results.note: Every value matches at the stated places. 37 not seeking treatment and 41 controls; 6.9 days of abstinence with urine negative on testing days (Participants 1st paragraph). Grades before self-reported first use (Academic records; Table 1 note). GPA 2.1 (0.7) vs 2.5 (0.6) and p = 0.016 (Table 1; Group comparisons 2nd paragraph). Age 34.0 vs 33.7, education 12.6 vs 12.7, estimated IQ 104.9 vs 105.0 (Table 1; the non-significance is stated in Group comparisons 1st paragraph). Model on age, parental income, smoking status and GPA with R2 0.41, d 0.61, t(36) = 3.732, p = 0.001 (Predictive modeling 2nd paragraph). Attention 0.69, p < 0.001; memory 0.46, p < 0.01; executive p = 0.87 (3rd paragraph). Editors' check recomputed: 3.732, 4.177 and 2.805 over sqrt(37) give 0.614, 0.687 and 0.461. The anchor rightly does not cite the executive d, whose printed -0.27 does not fit its t (card reporting issue 2). Role qualifies: right.

Numbers confirmed. Standardized to controls rather than published norms (Cognitive battery). d 0.54, t(36) = 3.302, p = 0.002 (Predictive modeling 4th paragraph). d 1.41, t(23) = 6.888, in the subset with test scores, 24 and 19 per Academic records and the Table 1 note (6th paragraph). 28 per group, d 0.71 (7th paragraph). Lifetime diagnoses 9/26, 0/12, 9/21, 0/9 (Table 1). Not causal, about 40% of variance, modest control sample (Discussion 7th paragraph). One wording correction: Discussion 4th paragraph says it is 'difficult to disentangle' methamphetamine from other substance use; 'cannot' applies only to telling the direction of the resulting bias with these data. Role qualifies: right.
results.corrected_extracted: Scores were standardized to the control group, not to published norms. The shortfall remained with withdrawal partialled out (d 0.54, p = 0.002), with standardized school test scores in place of grades (24 and 19 participants; d 1.41) and in grade-matched subgroups of 28 (d 0.71). Lifetime alcohol, cocaine, marijuana and other drug abuse or dependence: 26, 12, 21 and 9 of 37 in the methamphetamine group vs 9, 0, 9 and 0 of 41 controls. The authors state that effects of methamphetamine are difficult to disentangle from other drug use (their data cannot tell whether this leads to under- or overestimation), that the methods do not show a causal relationship, that the predictors explain about 40% of the variance, and that the control sample was modest for prediction.

results.corrected_locator: Methods › Data Sources, 1st paragraph; Results › SUDORS: Stimulant-Involved Overdose Deaths During January 2021–June 2024, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table, Overall (49 states and DC) row, methamphetamine columns; main-text footnotes §§ and †††
results.corrected_extracted: SUDORS, January 2021–June 2024, 49 states and DC (jurisdictions had to report at least 75% of their overdose deaths in at least one 6-month period; California and Wisconsin were included for part of the period, Texas and Wyoming only for January–June 2024, North Dakota not included): of 309,274 unintentional or undetermined-intent overdose deaths, 96,614 (31.2%) involved methamphetamine, meaning that the medical examiner or coroner listed it as a cause of death on the death certificate, in their report or in the postmortem toxicology report; 66,475 (68.8% of these; 21.5% of all deaths) also involved opioids and 30,139 (9.7% of all deaths) did not. Any stimulant: 182,502 (59.0%), 73.0% of them with opioids.

Every number confirmed against the Table, methamphetamine columns. Circumstance N 67,831 (46,985 with and 20,846 without opioids). Limitations paragraph (first and second limitations; 'underestimation'); Results SUDORS 3rd paragraph (46 states and DC; methamphetamine patterns comparable). One correction: the age rows sit in the Table's Overall section (all 96,614 methamphetamine-involved deaths, 49 states and DC), not among deaths with circumstance data, so the corrected text gives the age contrast its own population. Note that the contrasts are crude (no age standardization). Role qualifies: right.
results.corrected_extracted: Among methamphetamine-involved deaths with circumstance data (46 states and DC; 67,831 deaths), those without opioids more often had a known history of cardiovascular disease (hypertension excluded; 39.3% vs 19.8%) and were more often seen in an emergency department for the fatal overdose (30.3% vs 17.4%), and less often had evidence of opioid use (12.2% vs 41.1%). Among all methamphetamine-involved deaths (49 states and DC), those without opioids were older (aged 45–54, 55–64 and 65 or older: 27.1%, 27.9% and 9.2% vs 21.3%, 14.3% and 3.2%). The authors expect stimulant-involved deaths to be underestimated: some are certified with cardiovascular causes and get no overdose code, and postmortem toxicology varies and does not routinely test for emerging stimulants.
